arsenal-title-defence:
The fact that starts the season

Arsenal are the defending Premier League champions. BBC Sport, in the official fixture coverage, recorded that Mikel Arteta led them to their first Premier League title since 2004. Their defence begins at home to newly promoted Coventry City on Friday 21 August, 20:00 BST, live on Sky Sports. The Premier League made that the first match of 2026/27.

What they have already won in August

On 16 August Arsenal beat Manchester City 3–0 in the FA Community Shield at the Principality Stadium. The FA named Riccardo Calafiori, Kai Havertz and Martin Ødegaard as the scorers, timed the first goal at 24 seconds, and noted Arsenal have now won the Shield for the second time in three years. The Community Shield is a real trophy and a real result. It is also not a Premier League match. It does not move anyone up a table that has not started.

Who they open against

Coventry City won the Championship. At the Premier League AGM they were entered into the share register as members. BBC Sport says Friday is their first top-flight match in 25 years. Champions against a club that has waited a quarter of a century: that is the opening night the fixture computer produced. It is not a claim about how easy or hard the afternoon will be.

The rest of their opening stretch is also published

The Premier League released the full opening-round list on 19 June. After Coventry, Arsenal's next published league matches sit on that same calendar — kick-off times later in the season still move for television and for Europe. This page is about the Friday that actually starts the defence. For the whole confirmed season calendar, including who came up and who went down, use the 2026/27 season guide.

The question this page will not answer

The draft title asked whether anyone can stop Arsenal. That is a season question. Two days before kick-off, nobody has played a league minute. BRYME will not publish a predicted table, a 'who can stop them' ranking, or an invented injury list. The match page for Arsenal v Coventry will carry the result after full-time. Until then the confirmed record is: they are champions, they have the Shield, and they host Coventry on Friday night.
ballon-dor-race:
What is confirmed

The 2026 Ballon d'Or ceremony will be held in London on 26 October. UEFA announced the date and city on 28 May 2026. It is the 70th edition of the award France Football created in 1956, and the first time the ceremony has been staged in London.

UEFA said the choice of city pays tribute to Sir Stanley Matthews, the first winner, 70 years earlier.

The award is presented by France Football (L'Équipe Group) and has been co-organised with UEFA since 2024. Official notices sit on ballondor.com.

Who holds it now

The 2025 men's Ballon d'Or went to Ousmane Dembélé (France, Paris Saint-Germain). The 2025 women's Ballon d'Or went to Aitana Bonmatí (Spain, Barcelona). UEFA published both results on 22–23 September 2025.

Those are last year's winners. They are not this year's.

How the vote works

UEFA's official 2025 results page sets out the method. An international jury of specialised journalists votes — one from each of the top 100 FIFA-ranked nations for the men's award, and the top 50 for the women's.

Each juror picks ten players from a 30-name list, in order. Those ten get 15, 12, 10, 8, 7, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 point.

That is last year's published method. If France Football changes it for 2026, the official announcement is the source — not this paragraph.

What last year's vote actually looked like

The 2025 ceremony was at the Théâtre du Châtelet in Paris on 22 September 2025 — the 69th edition, covering the 2024/25 season. UEFA published the points.

Men's Ballon d'Or 2025: 1. Ousmane Dembélé (France, Paris Saint-Germain) 1,380. 2. Lamine Yamal (Spain, Barcelona) 1,059. 3. Vitinha (Portugal, Paris Saint-Germain) 703. 4. Mohamed Salah (Egypt, Liverpool) 657. 5. Raphinha (Brazil, Barcelona) 620. 6. Achraf Hakimi (Morocco, Paris Saint-Germain) 484. 7. Kylian Mbappé (France, Real Madrid) 378. 8. Cole Palmer (England, Chelsea) 211. 9. Gianluigi Donnarumma (Italy, Paris Saint-Germain / Manchester City) 172. 10. Nuno Mendes (Portugal, Paris Saint-Germain) 171.

Women's Ballon d'Or 2025: Aitana Bonmatí (Spain, Barcelona) 506, ahead of Mariona Caldentey (Spain, Arsenal) 478 and Alessia Russo (England, Arsenal) 420.

Those numbers are last year. They are not a 2026 ranking.

What this page will not do

The 2026 winners have not been announced. UEFA's May note said the list of nominees would be communicated in due course. As of 19 August 2026, BRYME is not copying a newspaper power ranking or a fan shortlist onto this page.

We will not tell you who "really deserves" the award. We will not invent a 30-name list. If France Football or UEFA publish an official shortlist, that is when names belong here.

A World Cup summer sits inside the 2025/26 season this award covers. That will matter to voters. It does not let us name a winner in August.

What to open next on BRYME

The last tournament that will sit in voters' minds is already written up: Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time in the 2026 World Cup final. The Premier League season that started last week is on its own pages.

We have also published our own editorial ranking of the race — clearly labelled as BRYME's view, not France Football's. It is a prediction. It is not the official 30.

Come back to this briefing when there is an official list, or a result.
ballon-dor-2026-our-picks:
A race, not a result

The 2026 Ballon d'Or ceremony is in London on 26 October. UEFA confirmed the date and the city in May. It is the 70th edition. Ousmane Dembélé and Aitana Bonmatí still hold last year's awards. France Football has not published this year's 30-name list. The winner has not been named.

That does not mean the season left nothing to judge. The 2025/26 club campaign is finished. The World Cup is finished. Spain are world champions. Paris Saint-Germain retained the Champions League. Harry Kane won the European Golden Shoe. Voters will have to weigh those things against each other. Only one player can win the men's award. The rest of this page is our current prediction of who has the strongest case — not a UEFA ranking, not a France Football shortlist, and not a claim about who will lift the trophy in October.

If France Football changes the voting method, their announcement is the source. Last year, one specialised journalist from each of the top 100 FIFA-ranked nations picked ten names from a list of 30. Those ten received 15, 12, 10, 8, 7, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 point. That is how 2025 was decided. It is the method we are writing against, unless they say otherwise.

In our view, the strongest cases currently belong to five players. They are not equally likely. We ranked them.

Our current top 5

1. Harry Kane (England, Bayern Munich) — our No. 1. 2. Lamine Yamal (Spain, Barcelona) — the biggest threat to Kane. 3. Rodri (Spain, Manchester City) — the World Cup argument in one player. 4. Kylian Mbappé (France, Real Madrid) — the scoring case without the biggest trophies. 5. Lionel Messi (Argentina, Inter Miami) — still elite, and a finalist, not a champion.

Below is why we have them in that order, what each man actually did, and what would have to change for the ranking to move.

1. Harry Kane — our No. 1

Kane's 2025/26 season at Bayern is the cleanest individual scoring year in Europe. FC Bayern's own announcement put him on 36 Bundesliga goals and 72 Golden Shoe points, clear of Erling Haaland (27 league goals, 54 points) and Kylian Mbappé (25, 50). He scored 61 times in 51 appearances in all competitions. After the domestic double — league and DFB-Pokal — he called it the best season of his career. Bayern said he scored a hat-trick in the cup final.

The Golden Shoe is his second. The first was 2023/24, also with 36 league goals. That is not a purple patch. It is a standard.

In Europe he was one goal off the Champions League scoring title. UEFA's official list has Mbappé on 15 in 11 matches and Kane on 14. Kane scored in the semi-final second leg against Paris. Bayern did not reach the final. Paris retained the trophy against Arsenal on penalties in Budapest. Kane's club year is a German double and a European near-miss, not a treble.

For England he reached a World Cup semi-final and lost it. Argentina came from behind in Atlanta: Anthony Gordon scored, Enzo Fernández and Lautaro Martínez answered late, 2-1. FIFA's Golden Boot table has Kane on six World Cup goals. Useful. Not decisive. England did not play in the final.

His strongest Ballon d'Or argument is the combination voters rarely get in the same player: unmatched league scoring, a second Golden Shoe, and actual club trophies. Numbers without silverware lose. Silverware without numbers looks like a supporting act. Kane has both.

His biggest weakness is the ceiling above the Bundesliga. He did not win the Champions League. He did not win the World Cup. A voter who treats those two competitions as the only stages that matter can leave him off the top of the ballot and still sleep.

Why he could win: because the season's scoring table is not close, and Bayern won the two domestic cups that were in front of them. Why he might not: because Yamal and Rodri can put a World Cup winner's medal on the table, and Kane cannot.

2. Lamine Yamal — our No. 2

Yamal's case is built on more than goals, which is the point. Barcelona's own season recap made him LaLiga player of the year after a title-winning campaign: 16 league goals, 11 assists, and no other player in the division provided as many passes that became goals. He shared the Zarra trophy with Ferran Torres. It was his highest-scoring league season. He is still a teenager.

Then he won the World Cup. Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time in New Jersey. Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute. FIFA recorded it. Barcelona called Yamal the youngest player ever to win both the European Championship and the World Cup. That sentence will follow him into every ballot conversation in October.

If voters place enormous weight on international success and on the player who makes a champion side more dangerous, Yamal can overtake Kane. Last year he finished second in the official men's vote, behind Dembélé, with 1,059 points. He already knows what a Ballon d'Or night looks like from the row below the winner.

His strongest argument is influence plus the biggest prize in the sport. A winger who creates as much as he finishes, in a league-winning side, then lifts the World Cup before he is 20, is not a sentimental pick. It is a coherent one.

His biggest weakness is the raw scoring gap. Kane's 36 league goals and 61 in all competitions are a different sport from 16 and 11. Yamal did not win the Golden Shoe. Barcelona did not win the Champions League — Paris did. A voter who wants a centre-forward's numbers will not be argued out of Kane by a highlight reel.

Why he could win: because the World Cup still moves this award, and Yamal was not a passenger in Spain's. Why he might not: because Kane's season is easier to put on a spreadsheet, and some ballots still look like spreadsheets.

3. Rodri — our No. 3

Rodri's case is a different sport again. FIFA gave him the adidas Golden Ball as the outstanding player of the 2026 World Cup. Spain won all the way through, conceded one goal in the tournament — Belgium's Charles De Ketelaere — and beat Argentina in extra time. FIFA's own write-up of the champions put Rodri at the centre of that control: when he raised the tempo, Spain raised it; when he broke the other side's rhythm, the team stayed in shape.

That is not a goals-and-assists argument. It is the argument that the most important player in the world champions is the most important player of the year. Rodri already won this award in 2024. He knows the room.

His strongest Ballon d'Or case is simple to say and hard to measure: he was the midfielder the World Cup was built around, and FIFA's technical group agreed. You cannot watch Spain's tournament and pretend the No. 16 was furniture.

His biggest weakness is the same fact, flipped. Forwards leave numbers that travel across languages. Rodri leaves control. Last year's official top ten was almost entirely attackers and creators. A midfielder has to be obviously the best player at the biggest tournament to break that habit. He was. Whether 100 journalists, filling in ten names in a hotel the week the shortlist drops, will all see it the same way is another question.

We do not have a clean official account of his club scoring that belongs on this page, and we are not going to invent one. His Ballon d'Or case in 2026 runs through Spain, not through a Golden Shoe table.

Why he could win: because the Golden Ball at a World Cup is the loudest individual honour the sport hands out between Ballon d'Or nights. Why he might not: because Kane and Yamal give voters a simpler story, and simple stories get 15 points.

4. Kylian Mbappé — our No. 4

Mbappé has one of the strongest individual scoring years of anyone in this race. Real Madrid and UEFA both published the same Champions League line: 15 goals in 11 matches, top scorer, including 13 in the league phase — a record for that stage — and a goal in each quarter-final leg against Bayern. Only Cristiano Ronaldo has scored more in a single Champions League season. Bayern still knocked Madrid out.

In the league he finished third on the Golden Shoe list with 25 goals. That is elite. It is also 11 behind Kane.

At the World Cup he won the adidas Golden Boot. FIFA's official scoring table has him on 10 goals and four assists. He also took the Bronze Ball. France did not take the trophy. They lost to Spain in the semi-final and then lost the third-place match to England. FIFA's own recap put France fourth.

His strongest argument is volume in the two competitions that travel: the Champions League scoring title and the World Cup Golden Boot in the same year. Very few players ever hold both conversations at once.

His biggest weakness is the trophy cabinet for 2025/26. Real Madrid did not win the Champions League. France did not win the World Cup. Kane has a domestic double. Yamal and Rodri have a world title. Mbappé has individual prizes and a fourth-place medal. That is not nothing. It is not the same as winning the thing the year is named after.

Why he could win: because some ballots still follow the top scorer, and he was the top scorer in Europe's biggest club competition and at the World Cup. Why he might not: because the players above him can point to a league title, a cup, or a World Cup, and he cannot.

5. Lionel Messi — our No. 5

Treat this case with the respect the year earned. Messi played in a sixth World Cup. Inter Miami's official tournament recap has him in all eight of Argentina's matches, with eight goals and four assists, through to the final. FIFA's Golden Boot table matches those eight goals. He took the Silver Ball, behind Rodri, and the Silver Boot, behind Mbappé. Argentina were the defending champions. They left New Jersey as runners-up.

The individual production is still ridiculous at his age. A hat-trick in the opener against Algeria. The all-time World Cup scoring record, broken during the group stage. Two assists in the semi-final comeback against England. Then a final he did not win. Spain's extra-time goal ended the defence of the trophy.

His strongest argument is that he remained the attacking reference point of a team that reached the last night of the World Cup, and that the numbers still look like a prime. Creativity did not dry up because the calendar said 2026.

His biggest weakness is the result that night, and the league he plays in. Reaching a World Cup final without winning it is a magnificent year and a harder Ballon d'Or year. The players above him either scored more in Europe, won their domestic league, or won the tournament. We are not going to invent an MLS scoring line to pad this section. His 2026 case is the World Cup. The World Cup ended 1-0 to Spain.

Why he could win: because a generation of journalists has watched him decide nights like this before, and eight goals to a final is not a farewell tour. Why he might not: because the award, in our view, should not go to the second-best team at the World Cup when the first-best team has Yamal and Rodri on the same ballot, and when Kane's club season is sitting there in plain sight.

Who has the strongest case?

The live argument is Kane against Yamal against Rodri. Mbappé and Messi are in the race. They are not, in our current ranking, about to win it unless the three above them all lose the room.

Kane against Yamal is volume against occasion. Kane has the Golden Shoe, the 61-goal club year, and a domestic double. Yamal has a league title, the league's player-of-the-season award, and a World Cup. If you think the Ballon d'Or is a season MVP for club football in Europe, Kane is ahead. If you think it is a prize for the footballer who most changed the biggest nights, Yamal is close enough to steal it.

Rodri against both of them is a category error on purpose. He will not beat Kane on goals. He will not beat Yamal on spectacle. He can beat both if enough voters decide that Spain's tournament was the event of the year and that he was the reason it looked inevitable. FIFA already made that call with the Golden Ball. The Ballon d'Or jury is larger, and more attached to forwards.

That is why Kane currently leads our editorial ranking. His year is the one you can defend in a single sentence without hedging: best scorer in Europe, champion in Germany, twice. Yamal's sentence needs a second clause about the World Cup. Rodri's sentence needs the listener to care about midfield. We care. We still have Kane first.

The picture can change. An official 30-name list from France Football would tell us who is actually on the ballot. A change in the voting method would tell us how those names are scored. Neither has been published as of 19 August 2026. Until it is, this is our view of the evidence in front of us — not theirs.

Final verdict

Our current pick: Harry Kane.

Only one player can win. Based on the club season that has actually been completed, the trophies that were actually lifted, and the World Cup that has already been played, Kane has the strongest overall case. Yamal is the player most likely to take it off him, because Spain won the tournament that will still be in voters' heads in October. Rodri is the player who makes the ranking honest: if the award is for the most important footballer of the year, not the most prolific, he is in the conversation whether the table likes it or not.

This is our assessment, not an official Ballon d'Or ranking. The ceremony is in London on 26 October. Come back when France Football names the 30, or when someone lifts the thing. Until then, Kane is where we would put the 15 points.

Liverpool said Iraola arrived after three Premier League seasons at AFC Bournemouth, and that he led Bournemouth into Europe for the first time with a sixth-placed finish.

What the club said about his path

Liverpool's announcement sketched the career it was hiring. Iraola, then 43, made more than 500 appearances for Athletic Club over 12 seasons, mainly as a right-back, and won seven caps for Spain. He finished his playing days at New York City FC. His first managerial job, the club said, was AEK Larnaca in 2018. Then Mirandés, then Rayo Vallecano — whom he led to promotion to La Liga in his first season — and then Bournemouth. The club staff page later summarised those Bournemouth seasons as consecutive finishes of 12th, ninth and sixth.

Iraola told Liverpoolfc.com he was “really excited”, and that Liverpool is “a big club, a massive club, one of the biggest in the world.” He talked about the atmosphere, the supporters and “the chance to fight for titles.” That is a first-day quote on the club website. It is not a tactical plan and it is not a guarantee.

Iraola's first Premier League match as Liverpool head coach is away at Newcastle United on Sunday 23 August, 16:30 BST, live on Sky Sports. That fixture is on the official opening-round list released by the Premier League. It has not been played. There is no result, no lineup and no post-match to write.

It does not list summer incomings or outgoings — those belong on the transfer tracker only when a club confirms them. The draft title asked whether Liverpool can challenge again. That is a question for May. In August the confirmed facts are a new head coach, a public first interview, and a Sunday trip to Newcastle.

champions-league-format-explained:
One table, not eight groups

From the 2024–25 season the Champions League abandoned the group stage it had used for three decades. Instead of eight groups of four, all 36 clubs now sit in a single league table.

The number of participants rose from 32 to 36. Each club plays eight matches — four at home, four away — against eight different opponents, and never plays the same team twice. Points work exactly as they do in a domestic league: three for a win, one for a draw.

The format is drawn from the Swiss system used in chess tournaments, where players are matched by strength rather than sorted into fixed pools. For the draw, the 36 clubs are divided into four seeding pots by UEFA club coefficient, and each team is drawn against two opponents from each pot, playing one home and one away in each pairing.

The league phase runs from September to January. The knockout rounds begin in February.

What the table decides

When the eight matches are done, the single table splits three ways.

Positions 1 to 8 go straight into the round of 16. They skip February entirely and enter the draw as seeded teams.

Positions 9 to 24 enter a two-legged knockout play-off round in February — eight ties for the remaining eight places in the last 16. Teams finishing 9th to 16th are seeded in that draw; teams finishing 17th to 24th are not.

Positions 25 to 36 are eliminated. This is the change that most altered the competition's stakes: under the previous format, third place in a group meant a drop into the Europa League. Now the bottom twelve are out of European football for the season, with no parachute.

Finishing ninth and finishing twenty-fourth both mean the play-off round, but they are not the same outcome. The seeding advantage runs all the way through the bracket.

Why league position still matters after the league phase

The knockout bracket is shaped by where you finished, and the advantage compounds.

Higher-ranked sides get the second leg at home — in the play-off round for those seeded 9th to 16th, and in the round of 16 for the top eight. The top four in the league phase carry that advantage into the quarter-finals, and the top two into the semi-finals.

The top eight are also paired in the draw so that the sides finishing first and second land on opposite sides of the bracket, meaning the two best league-phase records cannot meet before the final.

One useful wrinkle: if an unseeded club knocks out a seeded one, it inherits that seeding position for the rest of the run. The bracket keeps its shape even when the favourites do not survive it.

Getting in: the qualifying rounds nobody watches

The 36 clubs in the league phase do not all arrive the same way, and most of the field is settled long before September.

Twenty-nine teams qualify in advance: the Champions League and Europa League title holders, the champions of the ten highest-ranked associations, runners-up from the top six, third-placed teams from the top five, fourth-placed teams from the top four, and two places awarded to the associations with the best one-year coefficient.

The remaining seven come through qualifying, which begins in early July — before most domestic seasons have even started. Qualifying is split into two separate streams: a Champions Path for teams that won their national league, and a League Path for those who qualified by finishing second, third or fourth. Five of the seven places go to the Champions Path and two to the League Path.

That split is deliberate. It protects a route into the competition for champions of smaller associations, who would otherwise be drawn against clubs from far stronger leagues at every stage.

What the format changed in practice

Three things are measurably different.

More matches. Guaranteed group-stage football went from six matches to eight. A club reaching the final can now play up to 17 matches in the competition, against a previous maximum of 13.

More variety of opponent. Eight different opponents rather than three played twice means a wider spread of fixtures, and it removes the dead rubber — the final group game between two teams who had already settled their fate.

Harsher elimination. Finishing outside the top 24 ends your European season outright.

The honest caveat: whether the format is better is an argument about taste and calendar congestion, not a question with a factual answer. What is not in dispute is that clubs now need deeper squads. Eight matches against eight different opponents inside ten weeks cannot be navigated with the small core that a four-team group allowed.
champions-league-records:
The competition, briefly

The competition was established in 1955 and was called the European Cup until it was renamed ahead of the 1992–93 season. Every record below spans both eras, because they are the same trophy and the same lineage.

In seventy years, 24 clubs have won it.

Most titles: Real Madrid, and it is not close

Real Madrid hold fifteen titles, including the very first edition in 1956.

They also hold the record for consecutive wins, with five straight titles from 1956 to 1960 — a run that has never been approached since, and which the current format makes structurally harder to repeat.

By country, Spain has produced the most champions with twenty wins from just two clubs. England has fifteen wins from a record six different clubs — the widest spread of any nation. Italy has twelve from three.

That English figure comes with an asterisk that is part of the record: English clubs were banned from European competition for five years after the Heysel disaster in 1985.

The multiple-winner badge

A club that wins the competition three times in a row, or five times in total, earns the multiple-winner badge worn on the shirt in European competition.

Six clubs have earned it: Real Madrid, Ajax, Bayern Munich, AC Milan, Liverpool and Barcelona.

There used to be a second prize attached. Until 2009, a club reaching that threshold was allowed to keep the European Champion Clubs' Cup itself, and UEFA commissioned a new one. Since 2009 the winners each year receive a full-size replica and UEFA retains the original trophy.

The records nobody wants

Juventus have lost seven finals — more than any other club.

Atlético Madrid are the only side to have reached three finals without ever winning the trophy. Reims, Valencia and Arsenal have each finished runners-up twice without winning it.

And then there is the cruellest category in the competition's history. The venue for the final is chosen years in advance, and on four occasions a club has reached a final scheduled for its own stadium.

Two of them took the chance. Real Madrid won their second European Cup at the Santiago Bernabéu in 1957, and Inter Milan won their second at the San Siro in 1965.

The other two lost — both on penalties. Roma were beaten by Liverpool at the Stadio Olimpico in 1984, and Bayern Munich were beaten by Chelsea at the Allianz Arena in 2012.

The current holders

Paris Saint-Germain are the reigning champions, having won the 2026 final 4–3 on penalties against Arsenal after a 1–1 draw following extra time.

It is PSG's second title. For Arsenal it was a second final lost without a win — which is how they join Reims and Valencia in the runners-up column above.

A note on how these records are counted

Records in this competition are usually quoted for the combined European Cup and Champions League era, which is why Real Madrid's total includes titles from the 1950s and why Ajax's badge rests substantially on the early 1970s.

Appearance and goalscoring records are counted differently by different sources depending on whether qualifying rounds are included, so they are deliberately left out here rather than quoted with a caveat that most readers will not notice. The club records above are drawn from the finals record itself, where the count is unambiguous.
premier-league-2026-27-season-guide:
When it starts

Why the season starts so late this year

The 2026 World Cup pushed everything back. The Premier League's opening match falls 34 days after the World Cup final in the United States.

That compression shows up in the structure of the season rather than in the number of games. community-shield-2026-arsenal-manchester:
The result

Arsenal beat Manchester City 3-0 at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Sunday 16 August 2026 to win the FA Community Shield.

Riccardo Calafiori scored inside the opening minute, finishing after being played in by Myles Lewis-Skelly. Kai Havertz made it two on 28 minutes from a Christos Tzolis delivery. Martin Odegaard added the third two minutes into the second half, again set up by Tzolis, taking the ball round Gianluigi Donnarumma before finishing.

Samuel Barrott refereed. Odegaard, as captain, lifted the trophy.

Twenty-three seconds

The opening goal arrived before Manchester City had settled into the match — timed at 23 seconds by The Athletic, 24 by several other outlets. Either way, it is the first goal scored in the opening minute of a Community Shield since Bobby Owen did it for Manchester City against West Bromwich Albion in 1968.

That is the sort of statistic that usually decorates a report. Here it framed the whole afternoon. City spent the rest of the game chasing a match that had been shaped before they touched the ball properly, and they never really got hold of it. David Raya's most demanding moment did not arrive until Rayan Cherki tested him from range in the second half.

Arsenal's 3-0 is the biggest winning margin in a Community Shield since 2014 — when Arsenal beat Manchester City by the same score under Arsène Wenger.

Maresca's first competitive match

This was Enzo Maresca's first competitive fixture since replacing Pep Guardiola, and the first real look at Manchester City in the post-Guardiola era. It could hardly have gone worse. By the second half, Arsenal supporters were directing chants of “you're getting sacked in the morning” at him.

A Community Shield is, as TNT Sports pundit Joleon Lescott noted, effectively a pre-season game. His concern was the margin rather than the defeat: “the gap between the two sides in this particular encounter is probably as big as any gap between the sides I've seen in a long, long time.”

There were mitigating details. Erling Haaland had only recently returned to training after the World Cup and was withdrawn on 53 minutes. Several City players are short of match sharpness for the same reason. And Maresca's own response pointed at the squad rather than the performance — he said the sooner City can make signings, the better.

Ruben Dias, who captained the side, was blunter, telling TNT Sports: “It's the beginning of the season but it's not good enough.”

Donnarumma's afternoon will attract attention too. He fumbled the ball in the build-up to Arsenal's second and was comprehensively beaten by Odegaard for the third.

What it says about Arsenal, carefully

Mikel Arteta said the performance must set the “standard” for the season. That is a manager's framing, and it is worth keeping some distance from it.

What is factual: the reigning Premier League champions beat the FA Cup holders comprehensively, scored three, conceded none, and were still attacking at 3-0 rather than protecting the lead — Bukayo Saka came close to a fourth late on. Arsenal have now won four Community Shields in the last ten years.

What is not factual is anything about how the title race will go. This was one match in August between two teams at different stages of their pre-season, one of which has just lost the most successful manager in its history. A Community Shield has predicted very little historically, and this site is not going to pretend otherwise five days before the league starts.

What happens next

Arsenal begin their title defence on Friday 21 August at home to newly promoted Coventry City, the opening fixture of the 2026/27 Premier League season, kicking off at 20:00 BST.

Manchester City start on Sunday 23 August at home to AFC Bournemouth at 14:00 — Maresca's first Premier League match in charge.

english-champions-since-1888:
It starts with a meeting, not a match

The Football Association codified professional football in 1885. Three years later the Football League was established, after meetings initiated by William McGregor, a director of Aston Villa.

That is the actual origin of the English championship: not a grand founding vision but an administrator solving a scheduling problem for clubs who had just been allowed to pay their players and needed guaranteed fixtures to afford it.

The first season was 1888–89.

Preston won the first one without losing

Preston North End were the first English champions, and they completed their league fixtures unbeaten.

It is worth pausing on how rarely that has been matched in the 130-odd seasons since. Preston did it in the very first attempt, in a competition of twelve clubs, and it remains one of the few genuinely unrepeatable achievements in the sport — not because the football was harder, but because a twelve-team league no longer exists to be won that way.

The league was a northern competition first

For its first four seasons the Football League contained only twelve to fourteen clubs, and every one of them came from the North of England or the Midlands.

This was not a quirk of geography. Professionalism had been embraced more readily in the North and the Midlands than in the South, where the amateur tradition held on longer. The southern clubs that now dominate the English game were, at the point the championship was invented, not part of it at all.

The league expanded in 1892 by absorbing its rival, the Football Alliance. With 28 members it split into two divisions: most former Alliance clubs went into the new Second Division, the original league became the First Division, and promotion and relegation between them began.

That structure — a top division you can be thrown out of — is now so fundamental to English football that it is easy to forget it was an administrative consequence of a merger.

Two changes that moved the money

The two developments that most shaped who wins the title were financial, not sporting.

In 1961 the rules imposing a maximum wage on players were abolished. The effect was immediate and structural: power shifted towards the bigger clubs, because for the first time they could convert greater revenue directly into better players. Before 1961 a wealthy club could not simply outbid a poorer one for a footballer's signature. After it, they could.

In 1992 the clubs then in the First Division defected to form the FA Premier League, which became the new top tier. A series of progressively larger television contracts has since put unprecedented wealth into the hands of top-flight clubs.

Both changes did the same thing in different eras: they widened the gap between what the richest clubs could spend and what everyone else could. Every debate about competitive balance in English football traces back to one or both.

Who has actually won it

Twenty-four clubs have been English champions.

Liverpool and Manchester United share the record with 20 titles each.

The current champions are Arsenal, who won the 2025–26 title — their 14th English championship.

The spread matters as much as the top of the list. Twenty-four different winners across more than a century sounds competitive, and in the early decades it was; the concentration is a recent phenomenon, and it lines up closely with the two financial changes above rather than with anything that happened on a pitch.

A note on counting

Title counts in English football combine three competitions that are really one lineage: the Football League from 1888 to 1892, the Football League First Division from 1892 to 1992, and the Premier League from 1992 onwards.

This is why you will sometimes see two different numbers quoted for the same club — one counting all English championships, the other counting only Premier League titles since 1992. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. Every figure on this page is the full count across all three eras, which is the standard used in the official record.
world-cup-2026-spain-champions:
The final

Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time in the 2026 World Cup final on Sunday 19 July 2026, at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey — branded New York New Jersey Stadium for the tournament.

The game was goalless after 90 minutes. Ferran Torres, on as a substitute, scored the only goal in the 106th minute.

It is Spain's second World Cup, after 2010. Argentina, the holders, could not retain it.

A final decided by one substitute

A 1-0 scoreline after extra time invites the word cagey, and that is not quite what this was. Spain carried the game for long stretches and the goalless first 90 minutes reflected finishing and resistance rather than mutual caution.

The decisive contribution came off the bench. Torres was not in the starting eleven and settled a World Cup final — the kind of detail that tends to survive in the memory longer than the tactical shape either side started in.

For Argentina it ended a defence that had run to the last kick of the tournament. Lionel Messi's involvement gave the occasion a weight beyond the result itself, and the coverage of the night reflected that as much as it reflected the football.

What the 48-team format actually changed

This was the first World Cup played under the expanded format: 48 teams instead of 32, and 104 matches instead of 64.

The most consequential structural change was a new stage. Twelve groups of four fed into a round of 32 — a knockout round that had never existed in the tournament's history. Every previous World Cup went from groups straight into a round of 16.

Two practical consequences follow from that, and both are easy to miss in the noise around the winner.

The first is jeopardy arriving earlier for smaller nations and later for larger ones. A round of 32 gives more teams a knockout match, which was the point, but it also adds a round the favourites must survive.

The second is time. A 104-match tournament occupies more of the calendar than a 64-match one, and that has to come out of somewhere.

Where the time came from: your league season

It came out of the domestic season, and the effect is measurable rather than theoretical.

The 2026/27 Premier League season began on Friday 21 August — 34 days after the World Cup final. Both the start and the end of the English season are later than usual as a direct result, with the campaign now running to Sunday 30 May 2027.

The compression shows up in the shape of the season rather than the number of games. There are still 38 rounds, but they are arranged as 33 weekends and five midweek rounds.

So the tournament that finished in New Jersey in July is the reason your team plays a Tuesday night fixture in November. That is the clearest line you can draw between an international summer and a domestic winter, and it is worth remembering the next time a manager is asked about fixture congestion.

What we are not going to tell you

There is no player-by-player tournament rating here, no golden-boot table and no claim about which squad was deepest.

We covered the 2026 World Cup as it happened only in outline, and reconstructing detailed tournament statistics after the fact from secondary write-ups is how errors enter a site permanently. The facts above — the result, the scorer, the minute, the venue, the date, Spain's title count, the format — are the ones that are firmly established across the wire coverage.

Where BRYME did not verify something at the time, it does not appear here.

beginners-guide-to-making-money-online:
The uncomfortable opening

A phone, internet and free time can help you start learning, but they do not automatically turn into serious money. I spent time chasing gambling, betting, trading, make-money-online schemes and shortcuts because I wanted money quickly. The hard lesson was that the boring work people avoid — coding, writing, design and real practice — is usually where the long-term value is.

1. There is no holy grail online

Legitimate online work asks for skill, time, knowledge, creativity, problem-solving or consistent effort. Ask who is paying, what work is being done, why the payment makes sense, whether the model is transparent, and whether claims can be checked. “Make ₦500,000 in seven days with no skills” should make you suspicious, not excited. If you must pay before you can supposedly earn, treat that as a major warning sign.

2. Stop chasing quick money — build a digital skill

Coding, writing and graphic design are strong examples, not the only options. Video editing, digital marketing, data analysis, UI/UX, virtual assistance, cybersecurity and specialised AI-related work can also be useful. Earning potential tends to grow when your ability, experience, reputation and usefulness grow.

3. Test skills instead of waiting for the perfect one

Try coding, writing, design or another skill that interests you. Give each one focused time, then ask: does it keep my attention, do I want to return to it, can I practise it consistently, and am I willing to become good at it? ChatGPT can help you explore options based on your interests, but it cannot magically choose a career for you.

4. You can start with a phone

I started learning coding on a phone. A phone can be enough to begin many digital skills, although coding is slower and some tools or libraries are difficult to use without a computer. Do not wait for an expensive setup before you start; improve your equipment as your ability and income grow.

5. Learn without drowning in tutorials

Do not collect hundreds of random tutorials. Start with fundamentals, one concept at a time, practise regularly and ask questions when stuck. You can tell an AI tutor: “I want to learn coding. I am a complete beginner. Teach me step by step and make it easy and enjoyable.” Use AI to explain ideas, not to blindly copy answers. Documentation, books and courses remain useful as you progress.

6. Competence first. Income follows.

Do not spend your first months asking exactly when money will arrive. That pressure can make you rush past fundamentals. Learn, practise and become comfortable with the work first. There is no honest universal timeline for income.

7. When to seek paid work

You do not need to be an expert before taking a small job, but you must be able to deliver it properly. Appropriate routes can include freelance and remote-work platforms, writing opportunities, AI/data-work platforms, direct clients, local businesses and professional networks. Platform rules, assessments and availability change; none guarantees work.

8. Make your ability visible

Build a clear LinkedIn profile, CV, portfolio, demonstration projects and professional communication. Clients need evidence. A small project that shows what you can do is more persuasive than simply saying “I know how to code.”

9. Writing can be an entry point

If you communicate well, writing can be a practical starting skill. Clients may give a topic, length, style, deadline and payment terms; your job is to deliver useful work. AI can assist research, brainstorming, editing and structure, but it should not replace genuine thinking or produce junk. Rejected work may become portfolio material only when client rights and confidentiality allow it.

10. Do not take work you cannot do

Do not pretend you can deliver a high-paying job in a language or skill you do not know. Poor work damages trust, overwhelms you and can pull you away from the skill you were actually building. Choose work you can realistically complete well.

11. The first money may be tiny

Your first legitimate income may be cents, a few dollars or a small freelance payment. That is not failure. The point is to separate a small temporary task from building a capability that can lead to larger opportunities.

12. Treat microtasks with extreme caution

Microtasks can sometimes pay small amounts, but they are not a path to wealth. Never pay money to access a supposed microtask opportunity. Check rates, withdrawal requirements, country availability, minimum payout, terms and reputation. Some tasks pay very little for the time they take.

13. The biggest scam warning

“Make $100 every day with no experience”, “turn ₦20,000 into ₦500,000 in one week”, “guaranteed income”, “no skills required” and “pay to unlock your account” are reasons to stop and investigate. Understand the business model before giving anyone money.

14. Do not quit your job too early

A safer sequence is: normal job, learn a skill, small online income, more experience, more clients, consistent income, then financial stability. Do not abandon an existing income source because you have only started learning. Multiple income sources can be safer than one risky leap.

15. Upgrade equipment with a reason

Start with what you have. As income grows, improve your phone, laptop, internet or tools when they genuinely make you more productive. Do not go into debt for expensive equipment before you need it.

16. What consistency can make possible

Two or three years of serious practice can open possibilities: remote work, freelance clients, websites, software, digital products, a business or multiple income sources. My own coding journey eventually helped me build a website, a trading bot and other projects. That is personal experience, not a promise of the same result for everyone.

17. A skill can become more than a job

A valuable skill can grow from freelance work to clients, reputation, business, products and multiple income streams. That path takes time, proof of work and continued learning.

18. The hard part is consistency

Learning gets boring, frustrating, difficult and confusing. I felt that while learning coding. Treat each error as a puzzle to solve, one step at a time. Hard work does not guarantee wealth, but quitting every difficult thing guarantees you never get the chance to improve.

The BRYME conclusion

There is nothing wrong with wanting money. The mistake is believing money should arrive without value being created. If making money online was that easy, nobody would be doing the hard work. A phone and internet can open doors, but a valuable skill helps you walk through them. Stop chasing the shortcut. Build something valuable.
website-monetization-guide:
Build first. Monetize later.

Building a website that works, getting people to use it and monetizing it are three different jobs. A technically excellent site can make nothing if nobody visits. Before ads, know the audience, problem, reason to return and the model that fits.

1. Audience comes before monetization

The best investment you can make in a website is building its audience. Ad code alone does not create meaningful revenue. Visitor numbers, page views, location, engagement, time on site, returning visitors, niche and search traffic all matter. Advertising value varies; there is no honest fixed rate for every country or visitor.

2. Your niche matters

Research what people search for, the questions they need answered, advertiser relevance and whether a niche fits your intended monetization platform. Commercial demand can differ by topic, but no niche automatically makes money.

3. Getting your first audience

Start with search visibility: Google Search Console, a sitemap, useful search-friendly content, clear structure, mobile pages and internal links. Search Console helps submit, monitor and understand Google Search presence; it does not make a page rank. Early visitors can also come from WhatsApp, friends, Facebook, TikTok, relevant Reddit communities and other appropriate communities.

4. Give people a reason to return

One-time visitors are not the same as a real audience. Publish useful updates, build useful features, give clear reasons to return and consider subscriptions or notifications only where appropriate. The goal is for people to think, “I will come back later.”

5. Legitimate monetization options

There is no single best model. Google AdSense, alternative ad networks, direct advertising, affiliate links, products, services, memberships, voluntary donations and clearly labelled sponsored content can all fit different sites. Approval, earnings and availability are never guaranteed.

Google AdSense and alternative networks

AdSense can suit websites that meet Google’s current quality and policy requirements, but approval is not guaranteed and invalid traffic or invalid clicks are prohibited. Monetag and Adsterra are alternatives some owners consider; read each provider’s current official policies, formats, traffic rules and restricted-content rules before applying. Do not use one network to bypass another network’s rules.

Direct ads, affiliate links and your own offers

Direct sponsors can buy banner space, promoted placement or labelled sponsored content, with terms negotiated directly. Affiliate links may pay a commission for qualifying actions under a program’s terms and should be disclosed where required. A website can also sell products, services, tools, software or courses. Be clear about what is editorial and what is paid.

6. Do not monetize an empty website

“Welcome to my website. Here are five advertisements” is not a strategy. Establish useful content, navigation, a good experience and some returning visitors first. Establish the website, then monetize it.

7. Ads should not ruin the site

Ads are annoying when they are annoying. Intrusive placements can make people leave, stop returning and lose trust. Start conservatively, avoid covering important content or misleading placement, and test formats while following the provider’s current policies. Specific quantities are not universal policy.

8. Sustainable value beats maximum ads

More ads can create more opportunities but can also reduce reading, trust and return visits. The goal is not maximum ads. The goal is maximum sustainable value.

9. When to apply

Before applying, establish useful original or properly licensed content, clear purpose, functional navigation, good mobile experience, legal/policy pages, a legitimate audience and compliance with the provider you chose. Do not invent visitor or article thresholds; check official documentation.

10. Never buy fake traffic or click your own ads

Fake traffic wastes money, damages engagement and can cause invalid-traffic concerns, restrictions or termination. Never click your own ads, ask friends to click, create accidental-click traps, use fake download buttons or manipulate impressions. Real people who want your site are the only traffic worth building.

11. Copyright and honest placement matter

Do not copy articles, images, videos, logos or creative work without permission or compatible licensing. Use original, licensed or public-domain material where appropriate. Ads should look like ads, never fake navigation or site functionality.

12. If revenue is low, investigate

Do not panic or add dozens of ads. Look at visitor geography, page views, engagement, exits, niche, search intent, placement, formats, devices, seasonality and provider performance. Improve the website and strategy honestly; keywords alone are not a magic fix.

13. Diversify only when it fits

Once there is a strong audience, a site might combine ads with affiliate links, sponsors, direct advertising, products or memberships. It does not have to use every method. If users are happy and the current model works, unnecessary monetization can do more harm than good.

14. Do not get greedy after success

A healthy site can be ruined by extra ads, random niche changes, copyright shortcuts, fake traffic, click manipulation or chasing every revenue source. Once something works, protect it.

The long-term model

Build → Establish → Test → Publish → Grow audience → Earn trust → Monetize → Measure → Improve. Monetization is not the finish line. Keep improving the product and giving the audience value.

Final BRYME editorial

Build the website, establish it, test it, then give it to the world to see. Once the world loves it, monetize and get your pay. Do not build only to display ads. Build something people want, build real traffic, do not annoy visitors, and use the method that fits. Build the audience first. Monetize the value second.
freelance-platform-fees-explained:
The number in the blog posts is not the number on your invoice

Search for what Upwork charges and you will be told, confidently and almost everywhere, that it is a flat 10%. Search for Fiverr and you will be told the buyer pays 5.5% plus a $3 small-order fee on orders under $100. Both of those claims appear in fee guides published this year.

One of them is out of date and the other is wrong. This matters, because if you price your work off a number a content farm copied from a 2023 announcement, the shortfall comes out of your own pay.

So this guide does not cite fee calculators or comparison blogs. Every figure below comes from the platforms' own help documentation and legal terms, and the date each was checked is stated at the bottom. If a number here disagrees with something you read elsewhere, check the primary source before you trust either of us.

Upwork: not a flat 10%, and not the same on every contract

Upwork's own support article on the Freelancer Service Fee states that the fee "ranges from 0% to 15% per contract." There is no single platform-wide percentage any more. The fee is set per contract, based on factors Upwork describes only as supporting "a balanced and competitive environment across different types of work."

The practical consequences are more useful than the theory:

The fee is shown to you before you commit. Upwork displays the percentage when you submit a proposal or when a client sends you an offer, and you can see it later in the contract details and transaction summaries. You never have to guess which rate applies — but you do have to look, on every single contract.

Once a contract starts, the rate is locked. Upwork is explicit that once a proposal, offer or contract is sent, the fee will not change for that contract. What it will not do is stay the same across your other contracts.

The old tiered model is gone, and so is loyalty. The 20%/10%/5% sliding scale that rewarded long client relationships no longer exists. Billing a client for the hundredth time earns you no discount, and Upwork states plainly that it offers no regular discounts on the fee.

There are documented exceptions. Freelancers on Upwork Payroll pay no service fee, because they are paid through a third-party staffing firm. Any Hire contracts carry no freelancer service fee. Direct Contracts — where you bring your own client to the platform — carry a reduced fee. Enterprise client contracts are individually negotiated, though Upwork says freelancers working with Enterprise clients typically pay 10%.

The refund rule that almost nobody mentions

If money you were paid is refunded to the client, Upwork refunds the service fee you paid on that amount. Their worked example: $100 is returned to the client, your fee was 10%, so the $10 fee is returned to you.

This is a genuine protection and it is worth knowing before a dispute, not after. You are not charged a commission on money you did not ultimately keep. It does not, of course, refund your time.

Fiverr: 80% to you, stated in the payment terms

Fiverr is simpler and more expensive. Its Payment Terms, last updated January 2026, state that each completed order "credits your account with Earnings equal to 80% of the purchase amount." That is a 20% commission with no tiers, no volume discount and no loyalty reduction.

The same 80% rule is applied to hourly contracts: each completed weekly report credits you 80% of the hourly rate for the hours worked.

The one documented exception runs the other way, and it is unusual. Logo Designs sold through Fiverr's Logo Maker use a tier-based model where your share is a fixed percentage per tier, from 20% at the lowest tier up to 50% at the highest. Tiers are based on your Logo Maker sales over the previous twelve months and are recalculated on the first day of each month.

What your Fiverr buyer pays, and why it is your problem

The buyer-side fee is where the widely repeated numbers are wrong. Fiverr's Payment Terms state that as of September 2025 the service fee on gigs is 5.5% of the purchase amount, and that purchases under US$200 attract an additional US$3.50 small order fee.

Not $3. Not under $100. The threshold is $200 and the fee is $3.50.

That is a meaningful difference when you are setting package prices, because the small order fee is charged on a much larger share of orders than the popular guides imply. A $60 gig is a small order under Fiverr's actual rules; several fee comparison sites would tell you it is not.

Hourly contracts add one more line: a US$5 Order Initiation Fee on each new hourly contract, plus the 5.5% service fee on the hourly rate. The weekly billing cycle runs Monday 00:00 UTC to Sunday 23:59 UTC, with buyers charged automatically each Monday.

None of this comes out of your 80%. It still matters, because it is the number your buyer sees at checkout, and it shapes what they are willing to accept as your headline price.

Getting the money out

Fiverr publishes its withdrawal fees directly in the payment terms, charged by its payment service providers rather than by Fiverr:

PayPal costs US$0. The Fiverr Revenue Card, operated by Payoneer, costs US$1 within two days or US$3 within two hours, and is available worldwide except in India and Russia. Local Bank Transfer, also via Payoneer, costs US$3 per transfer and is available worldwide. Direct Deposit (ACH) costs US$1 per transfer and is US-only.

Two cautions that apply to anyone paid outside the United States. First, Fiverr notes that the provider you choose may apply additional fees based on your location and currency. Second, your Fiverr balance is always derived from its US dollar value, so the local-currency amount moves daily with exchange rates and includes conversion fees. You always have the option to withdraw in US dollars.

There is also a rule worth knowing before you ever need it: earnings from a disabled account can only be withdrawn after a 90-day safety period following full verification of account ownership.

Upwork's withdrawal options and their costs are documented separately from the service fee article cited here, and vary by country and method — check them against your own account rather than against any figure quoted in a guide, including this one.

Pricing so the fee is not a surprise

The arithmetic freelancers get wrong is subtracting the fee instead of dividing by what is left.

If you want to keep $20 an hour and the fee is 10%, you do not charge $22. You charge your target divided by 0.90, which is $22.22 — and this is exactly the example Upwork uses in its own documentation. Charging $22 leaves you $19.80.

The general rule: your rate equals your target take-home divided by (1 minus the fee rate). At Fiverr's 20%, keeping $100 means charging $125, not $120. At Upwork's maximum 15%, keeping $100 means charging $117.65.

Because Upwork's fee is now per-contract rather than fixed, this calculation has to be redone for each contract instead of once. Read the percentage on the offer screen before you accept it. Upwork provides a built-in rate calculator that estimates net pay after the fee, and it notes that rounding can shift the final figure by a cent or two in either direction.

What this does not tell you

Fees are the easiest part of platform economics to verify and the least important part of whether the work is worth doing.

This guide makes no claim about which platform will earn you more, how quickly you can expect a first order, or what a realistic income is. Those depend on your category, your portfolio, your competition and your timing, and anyone who quotes you a confident number for them is guessing.

What you can take from this: the commission is knowable, it is published, and it is different from what most of the internet says it is. Check it on the source, price by dividing rather than subtracting, and re-check whenever you start a new contract — because on Upwork the rate is now a per-contract variable, and on Fiverr the buyer-side thresholds have already moved once since September 2025.
writing-field-notes-how-this-works:
The only method that has paid me so far

I have chased the usual shortcuts. Writing is the thing that has actually produced money. Not because writing is easy, and not because the internet owes anyone a gig. Because a website that needs words will sometimes pay a person who can deliver them.

That is the whole idea behind BRYME Writing Field Notes. I research real publications. I write to them when I am going to talk about them. I publish what happened — including silence. Then, on YouTube, I walk through about three of those notes and how the money path actually works. If you want the dates, the apply links and the leftover sites from that month, they live on the field-notes page.

A gig is not guaranteed. Anyone selling you a script that skips this part is selling hope.

What this series is not

It is not a directory of every website that has ever had a write-for-us page.

It is not a promise that publications accept writers from Nigeria, or that they pay on time, or that they still run the programme you saw in a 2023 screenshot.

It is not a course. I will not ask you to pay to unlock a list.

If a row on the field-notes page does not have a date, treat it as unfinished. If I did not email them, I will not invent how long they take to reply.

The process, in the order I actually do it

First I pick a niche I can write. Tech explainers, money explainers, entertainment — only if I can produce a piece I would put my name on. Applying for medical or legal content I cannot stand behind is how you get rejected and deserve it.

Second I find the real door: a contributor page, an editor address, a form. I copy the URL. I read two or three of their recent pieces so the pitch is not generic.

Third I record the date I applied, what I sent, and what they asked for. That log is the product. Memory is how people start lying to themselves.

Fourth I wait. I do not send five follow-ups in a week. If nothing comes back, the note says “no reply as of this date.” That is a complete note.

Fifth, if they reply, I write down the brief, the pay if they named it, and the payment method if they named it. I do not upgrade “we will be in touch” into “I landed the gig.”

Country is not a bonus filter. It is the point.

Most public lists of “sites that pay writers” are written for people with a US or UK payment setup. From Lagos, the questions that actually matter are narrower.

Do they accept work from Nigeria, or do they quietly drop those emails? Do they pay through a method that arrives here, or only through a method that does not? Did they say any of this in writing, or am I guessing from a comment section?

I start these notes from Nigeria because that is where I write from. Other countries can be added later, the same way: one writer, dated applications, no copied reply times. If I do not know whether a site takes your country, the page will say unknown. Unknown is honest. “They hire worldwide” without evidence is not.

How money actually moves — when it moves

A typical paid path looks like this: you apply, they ask for a sample or a pitch, they give a brief, you write, they edit, they publish, they pay through the method they already use.

Any of those steps can stop. A killed draft is not a payment. A published piece with “exposure” and no invoice is unpaid work, and I will label it unpaid.

I will not publish a rate I did not see on their site or in their email. I will not publish a payout timeline I did not live. If their page is silent on money, the field-notes card will say unknown.

Earnings vary. The first legitimate writing money can be small. That is not a reason to buy a script. It is a reason to treat writing as a skill you practise, not a jackpot.

What I log for every site

Name and niche. The apply URL and the method — email, form, or pitch. Whether they say they pay, do not pay, or do not say. Payment methods they have named, if any. The country I wrote from. Whether I contacted them, and on which date. Whether they replied, and on which date. Whether I landed a gig, and whether I was paid. What they want, who should skip them, and what is still unknown. The date I last checked the page.

If a field would require a guess, I leave it empty and list it under unknowns.

The YouTube half

Each video covers about three sites I have already logged. The video should still be useful if you never open BRYME: what they publish, how I applied, what they said about money, and what happened in my inbox.

The website is for the parts that are awkward on camera — the exact links, the dates, the sites I researched but did not feature, and the updates when a programme closes.

I will not make “go to my website for the real list” videos that withhold the answer. If the answer is “they did not reply,” you will hear that in the video.

Why this is better than buying a script

A bought script is usually someone else’s voice, written for a different country, sold to people who do not want to send the email.

This method is slower. You will be ignored. You will write samples that nobody uses. You will also have a dated sentence you can stand behind: I wrote to them on this day, and this is what happened.

That sentence is reusable. A script is not. If writing never pays you, you still practised. If a script never pays you, you are only out of money.

Where the live list lives

The dated cards are on the Writing Field Notes page. This article is the rulebook. When a YouTube video goes up, the same page will carry the link.

I update a row when I re-check it. I do not delete a closed programme just to look current — a dated “closed” helps the next person more than a disappearing URL.

If you want the honest version of online writing, start there. If you want a guarantee, I do not have one.

The six rules that apply no matter where you are

  1. No legitimate platform charges you to join. Not for a “starter kit”, not for “premium access”. If a page asks for payment before you can work, it is not legit.
  2. Nobody needs your bank password. Payment setup only ever needs your PayPal email, bank account/routing number, or Payoneer/Wise — never bank login credentials.
  3. Unpaid assessments are normal — budget the time. DataAnnotation’s qualifying test is 1–3 hours with a low pass rate. Appen’s exams run 20–50 questions. Treat a failed assessment as data, not a loss.
  4. Pay is region-tiered — expect it. Identical work pays different rates by country. It is standard, it is not personal, and it is worth knowing before you start so the first payslip does not feel like a scam.
  5. Task availability beats hourly rate. The money is real but the queue empties unpredictably. Run 2–3 platforms, not one.
  6. “Legit but inconsistent” is not “not legit”. Complaints across these platforms are mostly about empty task queues, not stolen wages. That distinction is your most useful filter.

These patterns are enough to walk away from any page, platform or “mentor” claiming to get you rich:

  • Any upfront payment — “starter kit”, “premium access”, “registration fee”.
  • Requests for your bank login or OTP — legitimate platforms never need these.
  • “Make ₦500,000 in seven days with no skills” — excitement is the sales pitch, not the product.
  • An “Outlier”, “Appen” or other known-name page that asks for a fee or crypto — it is an impersonator, not the platform.
  • Pressure to act fast, or payment via gift cards or crypto to a “third party”.

Developers have their own lane: 20 verified coding & developer platforms with real rates, commissions and Nigeria payout notes (Payoneer, Wise, Grey, Cleva, Raenest beat PayPal, which remains limited for receiving in Nigeria). AI and microtask platforms are one lane. The other is paid writing: publications that pay for essays, fiction and reported pieces — many with no nationality restriction. For a Nigerian writer, the combination of a couple of AI platforms for steady income plus one or two paying publications for skill-building is the most honest “strategy” there is.

What actually works

Nothing on this page is a shortcut, because shortcuts are not real. What works is the same boring combination everywhere: build one useful skill (writing, coding, design, data, AI-assisted work), keep your profile honest, apply to several verified platforms, treat unpaid assessments as part of the process, and let reputation compound. What Outlier AI actually is

Outlier AI is an AI-training platform: contributors evaluate model responses, write and rank answers, and complete domain-specific tasks that help labs improve their models. For Nigerians it is one of the most accessible dollar-income platforms available — BRYME lists it as explicitly accepting Nigerian contributors, with payouts via PayPal or bank transfer.

The pay, honestly

Outlier advertises $15–100+ per hour. The realistic picture for a general contributor is an average of $25–38 per hour on active tasks, with specialist lanes (law, medicine, coding, advanced writing) reaching $50–100. Two honest caveats: pay is region-tiered — the same task can pay a US contributor more — and task availability swings. A week with a full queue can be followed by days of nothing. The pros run two or three platforms at once for exactly this reason.

  • 18+, with a valid government-issued ID for verification.
  • A PayPal or bank account for payouts — Payoneer and Wise generally work better for receiving dollars in Nigeria.
  • A laptop or smartphone; most evaluation work is comfortable on either.

Create an account, complete your profile honestly (this decides which project lanes you see), pass the unpaid assessments for the lanes you want, verify your identity, then wait for task invitations. Outlier never charges a joining fee, never asks for your bank login or an OTP, and never guarantees income. Any "Outlier Nigeria agent" asking for registration money on WhatsApp is running a scam on the platform’s name. The only official route is the platform’s own website.

Verdict

For a Nigerian with strong English and a laptop, Outlier AI is one of the better dollar lanes available in 2026 — with the queue-shaped caveat that it is an income stream, not a salary.
